title: Gene expression
lede: How a sequence of four letters in DNA becomes a working protein: transcription, translation, the genetic code, and how a single letter change causes sickle-cell disease.

sections.md:
## The central dogma
Information in cells flows in one main direction:

**DNA → RNA → protein**

- **DNA** is the master copy, kept safe in the nucleus.
- **Transcription** copies one gene into a message molecule, **mRNA**.
- **Translation** reads the mRNA to build a **protein**.

Think of DNA as the master cookbook locked in the library, mRNA as a photocopy of one recipe, and the protein as the meal.

## DNA vs RNA
| | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Strands | double helix | usually single |
| Sugar | deoxyribose | ribose |
| Bases | A, T, G, C | A, **U**, G, C |
| Job | long-term storage | carries and uses the message |

In RNA, **uracil (U)** replaces thymine (T). Base pairing: **A–T** (or **A–U** in RNA) and **G–C**.

## Transcription: DNA → mRNA
In the **nucleus**, the enzyme **RNA polymerase** unzips a gene and builds an mRNA strand complementary to one DNA strand (the template):

| DNA template | T | A | C | G | G | A |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mRNA | A | U | G | C | C | U |

The mRNA is edited (non-coding pieces called **introns** are cut out) and leaves the nucleus for the cytoplasm.

sections.q: A DNA template strand reads **GCA**. The mRNA is…
sections.why: G→C, C→G, A→**U** (RNA has no T).

sections.md:
## Translation: mRNA → protein
At a **ribosome**, the mRNA is read **three bases at a time**. Each triplet is a **codon**, and each codon specifies one amino acid.

- **tRNA** molecules carry amino acids. Each has an **anticodon** that pairs with a matching codon.
- The ribosome links the amino acids into a chain, which folds into a protein.
- **AUG** is the **start codon** (it codes for methionine). **UAA, UAG** and **UGA** are **stop codons**.

There are **64** possible codons (4³) but only **20** amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons. This redundancy means some mutations change nothing.

sections.title: Read a message
sections.answer: A tiny chain: **Met–Phe–Gly**. Real proteins are usually hundreds of amino acids long.

sections.md:
## Mutations
A **mutation** is a change in the DNA sequence.

| Type | What changes | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Silent** | one base, but the codon still means the same amino acid | none |
| **Missense** | one base → a different amino acid | ranges from harmless to severe |
| **Nonsense** | one base → a **stop** codon | protein cut short, usually nonfunctional |
| **Frameshift** | a base **inserted or deleted** | every codon after it is misread |

**Sickle-cell disease** is a missense mutation: a single base change in the hemoglobin gene swaps one amino acid (glutamic acid → valine). That one change makes hemoglobin clump, bending red blood cells into a sickle shape.

**Frameshifts are usually worst.** THE CAT ATE THE RAT, delete the first E: THC ATA TET HER AT… every "word" after the error becomes nonsense.

sections.q: Inserting one extra base into a gene usually causes…
options: a frameshift that scrambles every codon after it
sections.why: The reading frame shifts by one.

sections.md:
## Same DNA, different cells
Almost every cell in your body has the **same DNA**. A muscle cell and a nerve cell differ because they **express** (turn on) different genes. Muscle cells transcribe genes for actin and myosin; nerve cells, genes for neurotransmitter machinery.

**Gene regulation** decides which genes are transcribed, when and how much. Signals like hormones, diet and exercise can change gene activity. Training literally changes which genes your muscle cells express.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **mRNA uses U, not T.**
- **Codons are on mRNA; anticodons are on tRNA.**
- **Not every mutation is harmful.** Many are silent or neutral, and some are beneficial (the raw material of evolution).
- **Every cell doesn't have different DNA.** Different cells use different parts of the same DNA.

practice.q: How many bases in one codon?
A mutation that changes a codon to a stop codon is…

options: a single base substitution that changes one amino acid

practice.q: DNA template: **TAC CCG ATT**. The mRNA is…
practice.why: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C. Result: **AUG GGC UAA** = start, glycine, stop.
practice.hint: Pair each base, remembering A pairs with U in RNA.

practice.q: An mRNA coding region has 450 bases, ending with a stop codon. How many amino acids are in the protein?
practice.why: 450 ÷ 3 = 150 codons. The last is a stop codon, which adds no amino acid: **149**.

options: deleting one base near the start of a gene
a substitution that changes CUU to CUC (both leucine)
a substitution creating a stop codon early
practice.why: Same amino acid → silent. Redundancy in the code protects against some mutations.
practice.hint: Which one doesn't change the protein?

practice.q: A skin cell and a liver cell from the same person have…
options: the same DNA but express different genes
practice.why: Specialization comes from gene regulation, not different genomes.
